```{=html}
<p class="lx-eyebrow">From a law to rates, rules and permits (U.S. federal and Kansas examples)</p><div class="x4-branch"><div class="x4-root"><b>Law</b><span>Congress or a state legislature gives a regulator its authority.</span></div><ul class="x4-tracks" aria-label="Three separate tracks"><li><b>Market rules and tariffs</b><span>FERC writes rules for wholesale markets and transmission; an RTO or a utility files its tariff at FERC.</span></li><li><b>Retail rates</b><span>The state commission, in Kansas the KCC, decides each utility's rate case.</span></li><li><b>Project permits</b><span>A county, the state or a federal agency, depending on what is built and where.</span></li></ul><p class="x4-note">These approvals follow separate tracks and can overlap: one project may need a tariff change, a rate decision and permits at the same time.</p></div><p>Prairie Town's utility (fictional), in Kansas, wants a wind farm and a new 345 kV line (kV, kilovolts: the line's voltage) about 40 miles long, and to recover their cost in its rates.</p><p class="lx-eyebrow">One finished federal rulemaking, FERC Order No. 2222: six selected milestones</p><ol><li>19 November 2015: A panel at FERC's open meeting.</li><li>11 April 2016: Data requests and a request for comments (44 comments).</li><li>17 November 2016: A proposed rule (109 comments).</li><li>10 April 2018: A technical conference (52 comments).</li><li>17 September 2020: The final rule, Order No. 2222.</li><li>Then: Each RTO files its tariff changes.</li></ol><p class="lx-eyebrow">A Kansas rate case</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table x4-fbt"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Stage</th><th scope="col">Who</th><th scope="col">What happens</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Application (Day 0)</td><td>The utility</td><td>The utility files an application with supporting data; it needs the commission's approval to change rates.</td></tr><tr><td>Staff review</td><td>KCC staff</td><td>Staff examine the utility's books and records, ask for more data and recommend; the recommendation is not binding.</td></tr><tr><td>Testimony</td><td>The utility, staff, CURB and other intervenors</td><td>Expert witnesses file written testimony; the Citizens Utility Ratepayer Board (CURB) speaks for homes and small businesses, and other <span class="lx-term" data-term="intervenor">intervenors</span> may join.</td></tr><tr><td>Public hearing</td><td>Members of the public</td><td>Not required by law, but generally held in significant cases; public comments become part of the record.</td></tr><tr><td>Evidentiary hearing</td><td>The three commissioners and every party</td><td>When held, this <span class="lx-term" data-term="evidentiary-hearing">evidentiary hearing</span> presents the facts formally; commissioners review testimony and exhibits and may question witnesses.</td></tr><tr><td>Order (Within 240 days)</td><td>The three commissioners</td><td>In most cases the commission issues its decision, a written order, within 240 days of the filing; the limit can be waived in certain circumstances.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><details class="x4-qa"><summary>The utility, the commission's staff and CURB sign a settlement. Must the commission accept it?</summary><p>No: the KCC may accept, reject or modify a settlement; the commissioners decide.</p></details><p class="lx-eyebrow">Who decides</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table x4-fbt"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Decision</th><th scope="col">Level</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Rules letting small resources join SPP's wholesale markets as a group</td><td>Federal</td></tr><tr><td>The price per kWh a Prairie Town home pays its investor-owned utility</td><td>State</td></tr><tr><td>A siting permit for the new 345 kV line, about 40 miles long</td><td>State</td></tr><tr><td>Approval of where the wind farm's turbines may stand</td><td>Local</td></tr><tr><td>A check that the tall turbines are safe for aircraft</td><td>Federal</td></tr><tr><td>Mandatory reliability standards for the bulk power grid</td><td>Federal</td></tr><tr><td>A permit to put solar panels on a Prairie Town roof</td><td>Local</td></tr></tbody></table></div><details class="x4-qa"><summary>Which can any member of the public do?</summary><p>Both: KCC comments enter the case record, and FERC took 109 comments on the proposed rule behind Order No. 2222.</p></details><p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you put the rule's milestones in order, step through a rate case, sort who decides what and find where the public can speak.</p>
<!-- x04-fallback:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<!-- x04-ideas:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Separate tracks</dt><dd>A law gives a regulator its authority; market rules and tariffs, retail rates and project permits then follow separate tracks, which can overlap.</dd><dt>Who regulates what</dt><dd>FERC regulates interstate transmission and wholesale sales; state commissions such as the KCC approve retail rates.</dd><dt>Dates</dt><dd>One federal rule, Order No. 2222, took 4 years and 9 months from first panel to final rule; a Kansas rate case runs on a 240-day decision clock in most cases.</dd><dt>Voices</dt><dd>Rulemakings take comments; rate cases take testimony from parties and comments from the public; the commissioners decide.</dd><dt>Siting</dt><dd>Where turbines may stand is decided mostly by local governments, sometimes with the state.</dd></dl>
<!-- x04-ideas:end -->
</div>
</div>
<!-- x04-stop:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-card xs-stop" id="x04-stop"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Where we stop</p><h3>This side topic stops at how rules are made</h3><p class="xs-stop-lede">Rules enter the course as who decides what, in what order and when; reading legal texts and following live cases is the work of lawyers and regulatory staff.</p><div class="xs-stop-cols"><div><h4 class="xs-h">This side topic covers</h4><ul><li>Who makes which rule: Congress and FERC, a state legislature and its commission, counties and cities.</li><li>How a law leads, on separate tracks, to market rules and tariffs, retail rates and permits, and where the public can take part.</li><li>Reading dates: one finished federal rulemaking and a state commission's rate-case clock.</li></ul></div><div><h4 class="xs-h">Left to specialists</h4><ul><li>Legal texts, their interpretation and legal advice.</li><li>Live proceedings: today's open dockets and pending rules.</li><li>Other states' and other countries' procedures, which differ.</li></ul></div></div><h4 class="xs-h">Read next, three rungs</h4><ol class="xs-ladder"><li><b>Start here.</b> Chapter 2 explains who regulates wholesale electricity, who regulates retail rates and how the markets grew. <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2024-01/24_Energy-Markets-Primer_0117_DIGITAL_0.pdf">FERC, Energy Primer: A Handbook of Energy Market Basics</a>, January 2024</span></li><li><b>Go further.</b> A state commission's own guide to a rate case: the revenue requirement, rate design, hearings and settlements. <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://kcc.ks.gov/electric/how-rates-are-set">Kansas Corporation Commission, How rates are set</a>, undated, read 7 November 2026</span></li><li><b>Go deep.</b> Read one finished federal rule in full: its procedural history, the comments and the commission's answers to them. <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-09/E-1_0.pdf">FERC, Order No. 2222 (Docket RM18-9-000)</a>, issued 17 September 2020</span></li></ol></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>How a rate case builds a rate</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<!-- x04-deeper:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<ul><li><b>Step one: how much.</b> The commission sets a <span class="lx-term" data-term="revenue-requirement">revenue requirement</span>: the year's approved expenses, including depreciation (recovering past investment) and income taxes, plus an allowed return.</li><li><b>The return.</b> It is earned on the <span class="lx-term" data-term="rate-base">rate base</span>, the net value of what the utility has built, at a rate that blends the cost of its debt and its shareholders' return.</li><li><b>Step two: who pays it.</b> Rate design splits that amount among <span class="lx-term" data-term="customer-class">customer classes</span>, such as homes and businesses: fixed charges, prices per kWh and, for large users, demand charges.</li><li><b>Where to see it.</b> The KCC describes both steps in its guide; the bills that result are the subject of lesson A4.</li></ul>
<!-- x04-deeper:end -->
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
